note: Orexin antagonists carried the same sleep-EEG signal rat, dog, primate and human inside single papers, and orexin-deficient narcolepsy (Hcrtr2-mutant dogs, orexin-KO mice) framed the safety question before any patient was dosed.
label: Insomnia (orexin)

engagement.model: Rat EEG/EMG sleep recording (with dog EEG)
engagement.note: Almorexant reduced wake and raised NREM/REM in rats and dogs; the same paper showed objective EEG sleep signs in healthy men.
engagement.short: Rat and dog EEG sleep matched in humans
engagement.quote: Here we report that in rats, dogs and humans, somnolence is induced by pharmacological blockade of both orexin OX(1) and OX(2) receptors.
engagement.reason: Sleep EEG matched rat-dog-human in one paper
engagement.judgement: No human orexin-receptor occupancy has ever been measured (no clinical PET tracer), so the engagement read-out is the pharmacodynamic one the class relies on: EEG-defined sleep after a dose. The first published use of the rat/dog sleep-EEG model for an HCRTR2 antagonist and the first human comparison are the same paper, so the strip opens directly at 'same' with no untested gap (model_first_use_year = 2007). Reinforced for the target itself by Gotter 2016 (doi:10.1038/srep27147): the OX2R-selective MK-1064 increased NREM and REM in mice, rats, dogs and healthy volunteers (NCT02549027, NCT02549014), i.e. HCRTR2 blockade alone is sufficient across species. Abstract-level reading of the 2007 paper.

dose.model: Ex vivo OX2R occupancy in transgenic rats, tied to rat/dog/rhesus EEG dose-response
dose.note: Suvorexant gave >90% OX2R occupancy at 1.1 uM plasma in rats; sleep dose-responses in rat, dog and rhesus; no human comparison yet.
dose.short: Rat occupancy sets the exposure target
dose.quote: Examination of Suvorexant in radioligand binding assays using tissue from transgenic rats expressing the human OX(2)R found nearly full receptor occupancy (>90%) at plasma exposures of 1.1 μM.
dose.judgement: Merck's dose model was occupancy measured ex vivo in rats expressing human OX2R, linked to the exposure at which active wake fell in rat, dog and rhesus. The FDA pharmacology and clinical-pharmacology reviews for NDA 204569 do not mention receptor occupancy at all (0 hits in either text), so model_filed is false even though the EEG studies themselves were filed. Abstract-level reading.

dose.model: Ex vivo OX2R occupancy in transgenic rats, tied to rat/dog/rhesus EEG dose-response
dose.note: Human plasma for 65% OX2R occupancy (0.33 uM, scaled from rats) was crossed by the effective 10-20 mg doses and cleared by 8 h.
dose.quote: Observed clinical suvorexant mean plasma concentrations fell below the levels predicted to correspond to 65% OX2R occupancy, where sleep-promoting efficacy is predicted, by the 8 h post-dose time point for both the 10 and 20 mg therapeutic doses.
dose.reason: Occupancy threshold held at human doses
dose.judgement: The comparison is retrospective: rat and dog efficacy needed 65-80% OX2R occupancy; the paper scales that to a human plasma level (0.33 uM) and lays Phase 1 PK curves over it, concluding that effects 'would not be expected to persist into subsequent waking hours at therapeutic doses less than 20 mg'. The FDA then found only 15 mg free of next-day driving impairment and labelled 20 mg with a driving caution, so the exposure cut-off landed within 2x. The 'therapeutic doses' come from the patient dose-finding trial (NCT00792298, results posted 2014-11-14; Herring 2012) while the PK is from unregistered Phase 1 studies, hence subjects = mixed and registry_date null. Prospective confirmation came later for daridorexant: Treiber 2017 (doi:10.1124/jpet.117.241596) estimated an active dose of 25 mg from a ~65% occupancy threshold and reports the predictions 'largely confirmed' in the healthy-volunteer SAD study (Muehlan 2018, doi:10.1002/cpt.1046); not used for the status year. Note the FDA set the final suvorexant dose on human exposure-response, not on this model. Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC3765993).

efficacy.model: Rat and dog EEG sleep architecture (healthy animals)
efficacy.note: Rat/dog EEG showed more NREM and REM sleep without cataplexy; humans tested were healthy men, so no insomnia-patient comparison yet.
efficacy.short: Rat and dog EEG, healthy animals only
efficacy.quote: Here we report that in rats, dogs and humans, somnolence is induced by pharmacological blockade of both orexin OX(1) and OX(2) receptors.
efficacy.judgement: Scored untested rather than same because the human arm was healthy volunteers, not insomnia patients; the efficacy question is whether the disease responds. The model is healthy animals in their rest phase; Merck's own 2013 paper concedes 'translatable preclinical models for insomnia have not been developed'. Abstract-level reading.

efficacy.model: Rat and dog EEG sleep architecture (plus rhesus for suvorexant)
efficacy.note: Suvorexant improved sleep efficiency, WASO and sleep latency dose-dependently in 254 insomnia patients; almorexant did the same in 161 patients (Hoever 2012).
efficacy.short: Patients slept more, as rats and dogs did
efficacy.quote: Suvorexant showed significant (p values <0.01) dose-related improvements vs placebo on the coprimary end points of sleep efficiency at night 1 and end of week 4.
efficacy.reason: Insomnia patients slept more, as predicted
efficacy.judgement: Herring 2012 does not itself cite the animal data; the comparison is my juxtaposition with Winrow 2011 (rat 10-100 mg/kg, dog 1-3 mg/kg, rhesus 10 mg/kg all cut active wake and raised NREM/REM), which is the model the FDA pharmacology review names as filed. Hoever 2012 (almorexant, doi:10.1038/clpt.2011.370, 161 patients, NCT00640848 with no posted results) is the earlier 2012 patient comparison and points the same way. Direction only: animal end-points (active-wake reduction) and patient end-points (sleep efficiency, WASO) are not the same scale. Not 'neg': no HCRTR2 antagonist has failed on efficacy in patients; almorexant stopped for tolerability and filorexant for portfolio reasons, neither flagged by the model. Abstract-level reading.

safety.model: Orexin-deficient narcolepsy (Hcrtr2-mutant dogs, orexin-KO mice) as genetic anchor; rat/dog dosing watched for cataplexy
safety.note: Genetic orexin loss causes narcolepsy/cataplexy; acute almorexant produced none in rats, dogs or a few healthy men. No patient comparison yet.
safety.short: Narcolepsy genetics flag cataplexy; none seen
safety.quote: No signs of cataplexy were observed, in contrast to the rodent, dog or human narcolepsy syndromes.
safety.judgement: The paper does put rat, dog and human side by side on cataplexy (fact fields record that), but a handful of single-dose healthy volunteers cannot test a rare patient-level event, so the safety strip stays untested until the NDA. A re-scorer who accepts healthy-volunteer comparisons can move 'same' back to 2007 from the fields here.

safety.model: Dog food-enrichment cataplexy test (suvorexant-dosed) plus rat-occupancy carry-over prediction
safety.note: Dogs on suvorexant showed cataplexy-like limb buckling; patients got mild cataplexy-like symptoms. Next-day impairment at 20 mg matched the occupancy model's <20 mg cut-off.
safety.short: Dog cataplexy flag matched mild patient events
safety.quote: Symptoms similar to mild cataplexy can occur, with risk increasing with the dose of BELSOMRA.
safety.reason: Dog flag and dose cut-off both held
safety.judgement: Two predictions, both held. (1) Cataplexy: label 13.2 states that in dogs 'daily oral administration of suvorexant (5, 30 mg/kg) for 4-7 days resulted in behavior characteristic of cataplexy ... when presented with food enrichment, a stimulus demonstrated to induce cataplexy in dogs with hereditary narcolepsy', and the medical review records that 'nonclinical studies suggested a theoretical safety concern for cataplexy'; section 5.6 then warns of dose-related cataplexy-like symptoms in patients. (2) Next-day somnolence, the issue behind the FDA's cut from Merck's proposed 40 mg to 10 mg start / 20 mg max: the medical review says 'Suvorexant clearly causes dose related, next day effects, including sedation' and the clinical-pharmacology review concludes 'the only suvorexant dose, which did not cause next-day impairment on driving performance, is 15 mg'. Gotter 2013 (rat occupancy scaled to human PK) had published that effects 'would not be expected to persist into subsequent waking hours at therapeutic doses less than 20 mg', which is what the FDA found; but it appeared in August 2013, after the May 2013 advisory committee, and the sponsor's own proposed dose contradicted it, so it is a matched model, not a prospective save. If a re-scorer treats the NDA animal package's silence on next-day effects (no next-day endpoint in the pharmacology review; the rhesus residual-effect data were for DORA-22, not suvorexant) as a prediction that failed, this cell becomes contra. Almorexant: development stopped January 2011 after studies 'including tolerability'; the liver-enzyme attribution appears only in secondary sources and no animal-to-human hepatic comparison was ever published, so it cannot be scored and does not make this 'neg'. Registry date is the Phase 3 trials (NCT01097616/NCT01097629) whose somnolence rates the review quotes. FDA reviews and label read in full text locally.
